A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite the changed title and expanded scope. v1's two DAgger variants and theoretical guarantees remain identifiable in v2. The text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison.

before.justification: v1's main text and Appendices A–D contain algorithms, theoretical bounds, and proofs, but no original empirical results.

after.justification: Sections 3.2 and 4.2–4.3 and Appendix G report original synthetic-MDP simulations and continuous-control experiments, including returns and state coverage.

M1.justification: The original variants survive as STAGGER and TRAGGER. v2 adds WARM-STAGGER, which restricts the policy class using offline demonstrations before interactive updates, and the trajectory-wise WARM-TRAGGER variant (Algorithms 2 and 4). These introduce substantive procedures beyond renaming.

E1.justification: v1 has no empirical task coverage. v2 evaluates a constructed finite MDP and four continuous-control tasks: Ant, Hopper, HalfCheetah, and Walker2D. Appendix G specifies the corresponding BulletEnv implementations.

E2.justification: v1 compares analytical rates for LogLossBC, LogLossDAgger, and its proposed variants. v2 introduces empirical BC-versus-STAGGER comparisons and evaluates WARM-STAGGER against both. Appendix G.3 additionally compares TRAGGER and WARM-TRAGGER with the state-wise methods.

E3.justification: The new experiments introduce cost-matched budgets with C=1 or 2, sequential offline-data access, uniform state queries, and varying warm-start budgets. Appendix G specifies 20% held-out validation and evaluation over 25 rollouts every 50 annotations; the MSE experiment also uses a different learning rate. These are new protocols, not revisions to experiments in v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds state-coverage analyses of the synthetic MDP, sensitivity to offline-data budgets, MSE-versus-log-loss experiments, and state-wise-versus-trajectory-wise comparisons. These investigate cold starts, recovery, loss sensitivity, and annotation granularity; v1 contains no corresponding empirical analyses.

E5.justification: v1 has theoretical probability bounds but no empirical uncertainty reporting. v2 reports 10 random seeds for continuous-control experiments, 10th–90th percentile bootstrap confidence bands in Figure 1, and averages over 200 simulation runs in Section 4.2.

E6.justification: All empirical return and coverage curves are new. Figure 1 reports STAGGER matching or exceeding BC with fewer annotations; Figures 2–3 show benefits from selected hybrid warm starts. Appendix G.3 reports weaker trajectory-wise performance on several control tasks but similar performance between annotation modes on the toy MDP. These are newly reported comparisons, not performance improvements over v1 experiments.

T1.justification: v2 adds the hybrid cost formalism, each-step policy completion, Theorem 5's combined-data guarantee, and Theorem 7's separation construction with proofs in Appendices C–D. The original trajectory-wise and decoupled-Hellinger analysis largely survives in Appendix E. New theoretical documentation contains inconsistencies, including Appendix C's signs and horizon factors and Lemma 22's treatment of the returned policy.

C1.justification: The central contributions expand to hybrid learning that competes with either data source alone, strictly outperforms both on a constructed MDP, and offers empirical benefits under annotation-cost constraints. The earlier claim that trajectory-wise interactive learning matches BC remains in the conclusion and Appendix E.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving delayed feedback, cold starts, state coverage, and failure-induced resets. It qualifies benefits by annotation costs and offline coverage, and explicitly discusses uncounted environment-interaction costs, the expert-performance ceiling, and the gap between discrete realizable theory and continuous-control experiments.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's abstract algorithm descriptions, Appendix G supplies environment identifiers, expert and learner architectures, Gaussian-policy details, training and validation hyperparameters, evaluation procedures, hardware, and an implementation link. These substantially expand reproducibility information for the new experiments.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to adversarial and offline imitation learning, expert-intervention methods such as HG-DAgger and ThriftyDAgger, hybrid reinforcement learning, and warm-start contextual bandits. v2 distinguishes its heterogeneous-supervision setting from Hybrid Inverse Reinforcement Learning. Much of v1's mixing-policy and lower-bound discussion is retained in Appendix A.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten, and the paper and algorithms are renamed. Hybrid learning becomes a central section, while the former trajectory-wise analysis and several discussions move into reorganized appendices. A standalone conclusion and limitations discussion replace the earlier brief conclusion.

P2.justification: v1's analytical summary table is omitted. v2 introduces eight numbered figures with learning curves, uncertainty bands, and an MDP diagram reused in Figures 2 and 8; Figure 7 organizes paired comparisons. Algorithm displays are expanded and relocated, and the document adopts a substantially different conference layout.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful empirical evidence, uncertainty reporting, implementation details, and explicit limitations to v1's theoretical note. However, Theorem 7's proof in Lemma 22 argues expert-level performance for an updated policy, whereas Algorithm 2 returns a mixture including earlier policies. Theorem 5 and Appendix C also contain inconsistent signs and horizon factors. These unresolved issues affect central new guarantees, preventing a reliable net judgment of the empirical and documentation gains against the theoretical weaknesses.
